claims.text: The starting material is a powder mixture of Nb, Mo, Ta, W, and V with Group IV hydride precursors such as TiH2 or ZrH2.
The Group IV-containing powder mixture is inherently susceptible to oxygen uptake.
Hydride precursors should be thermally decomposed before sintering and hot extrusion.
Hydride decomposition should be performed under an ultra-high vacuum below 10^-6 Pa.
A heating rate of 5-10 °C/min to 800-900 °C is appropriate for hydride decomposition.
Hot extrusion should subsequently be conducted above 1200 °C.
Thermal decomposition of TiH2 or ZrH2 under vacuum releases hydrogen without introducing oxygen.
A low heating rate prevents rapid oxygen ingress from residual gases or surface oxides.
The proposed vacuum decomposition history suppresses oxygen diffusion and uptake.
Suppressing oxygen uptake inhibits nucleation or precipitation of brittle alpha-HCP phases.
Avoiding alpha-HCP precipitation prevents an increase in the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.
High-temperature extrusion densifies the alloy without catastrophic cracking.
High configurational entropy maintains or stabilizes a single-phase BCC solid solution during extrusion.
The proposed process produces a dense bulk refractory high-entropy alloy.
The processed Group IV-containing alloy will be a single-phase BCC material.
The processed alloy will contain no detectable brittle alpha-HCP precipitates.
The processed alloy will have a yield strength exceeding 400 MPa at 1600 °C.
The processed alloy's high-temperature performance will be comparable to or better than that of cast counterparts.
In conventional casting or standard powder metallurgy, oxygen uptake causes alpha-HCP precipitation, brittle behavior, and elevated transition temperatures.
The proposed method is applicable to Ti-, Zr-, or Hf-containing refractory high-entropy alloys for which hydride decomposition is feasible.
